name: Valencian nationalism
summary: Valencian nationalism (valencianisme) holds that the Valencians are a people with their own language, history and right to self-government, and works for a Valencian state or autonomy within a federal or plurinational Spain. Since Fuster in 1962 its mainstream treats Valencian and Catalan as one language; its parties split over whether the Països Catalans are one nation, and the Bloc Nacionalista Valencià took a Valencian-only course with sovereignty at its centre. Its sources record little on economic or social questions beyond language, territory, autonomy and fiscal fairness.
scope: Valencianism as a doctrine of national identity, language and autonomy: the 1918 Declaració Valencianista, Joan Fuster's Nosaltres, els valencians (1962), Joan F. Mira's revision (1997), Alfons Cucó's and Rafael Company's accounts, and the Bloc Nacionalista Valencià's own congress documents and presidents (2000-2021). It excludes Blaverism (anti-Catalanist regionalism) and does not borrow the positions of the Compromís coalition or of Spanish left parties on economics, society or the environment.

national-self-determination.rationale: Base 2 of the 1918 Declaration claims the Valencian people's right to constitute a state that gives itself its own constitution, and Villalonga's commentary states the principle outright: every nationality has the right to an independent or autonomous state; the 2000 Bloc congress made sovereignty the party's course and Company calls the Valencians' right to self-determination the idea Valencianism stands for.

right-to-secede.rationale: Valencianism claims the right to a state of its own, independent or autonomous (Villalonga on base 2), and the Bloc is sovereigntist; but its stated aim is autonomy and federation, and none of the texts frames a general right of regions to secede.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Base 3 of the 1918 Declaration holds the Valencian State compatible with a Spanish or Iberian federation, with a clear distribution of powers and a divided treasury; base 8 lets it pool with other states for specific ends while keeping its personality intact.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Base 3 says the Valencian State's own functions are exercised with full sovereignty and no outside interference, and the 2008 declaration calls the present statute only a partial recovery of self-government; powers that Madrid could withdraw contradict both.

minority-language-support.rationale: Base 5 of the 1918 Declaration demands cooficiality for Valencian, the 2008 declaration asks for a Valencianism that strengthens the language, and Cucó names the demand for the language's dignity and social diffusion one of Valencianism's three constant points; Company criticises governments that fail to require it in public employment.

single-official-language.rationale: The 1918 Declaration asks for cooficiality of Valencian and Castilian (base 5), and Company attacks a public-service law that made Valencian only a merit; a sole official language contradicts the movement's central language demand.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Martínez Sabater's commentary on base 1 argues that Valencians must cultivate, clean and fix their own language and keep the people's style, and the 2008 declaration asks for a Valencianism that fosters Valencian and the features of the national identity.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Fuster treats Valencian and Catalan as the same language whose regional names arose later, Mira calls it a simple verifiable fact that Valencians and Catalans speak the same language, and Company calls decades of linguistic secessionism complicit in substituting Castilian.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Fuster holds that Valencians, Catalans and Balearics form one people, one nation; Mira, whose book the Bloc adopted, says the shared language does not make one political nation, and Company records that the Catalan Countries as political nation was explicitly set aside by majority political Valencianism.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Fuster calls the unity of the Països Catalans a moral obligation and the only way to survive as a people, while Mira and the Bloc's majority reject a single political space and Company says explicitly that pan-Catalanism was set aside; the strands split on political unity across borders.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Martínez Sabater's 1918 commentary traces the Valencian type unbroken from the Iberian ethnos, while Fuster's account and Cucó stress a rupture of Valencian identity after 1707 that Valencianism had to repair, and Mira sets the origin in the medieval kingdom; adherents tell different stories.

culture-before-state.rationale: Fuster is reported preferring a Valencian-language school line to nationalist parties, while Company argues there is no merely cultural nationalism and that the 1918 Declaration was political from the start; the strands split on culture first or politics first.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Base 1 of the 1918 Declaration defines the Valencian people as the inhabitants of the three provinces, Fuster calls a provincial frontier an artificial split of the Valencian people, and Cucó contrasts Valencianism with provincialist blasquismo; this is the Valencian case rather than a general rule.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Villalonga's commentary on base 2 says the will of the inhabitants decides the limits of the Valencian state, including whether the Castilian-speaking west joins or leaves, as Requena once did.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Base 8 of the 1918 Declaration lets the Valencian State pool powers with other states of a federation, and the 2008 declaration and Company call for a Valencianism present from town halls to the European Union and keep its europeist outlook.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Company calls for a civic nationalism addressed to all five million Valencians whatever their origin or language and the 2008 declaration for an open, plural, integrating project; the 1918 text's racial vocabulary is the older strand.

direct-action.rationale: Company says Valencian nationalism should take part with absolute normality in the Spanish state's democratic institutions and calls imitation of radical Basque methods a grave mistake; the Bloc's record is electoral, with years spent seeking the 5 percent threshold.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Villalonga's commentary states that each nationality is entitled to an independent or autonomous state, and Cucó treats self-government within a plurinational state as a constant demand; the Valencian case is the movement's own.
